# Golden rule and universal ethics (`golden_rule_universal_ethics`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/ideas.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Scientific method & philosophical ideas (`ideas`)
- Core idea: Do not do to others what you would not want done to you; more generally, a rule of conduct is acceptable only if you would accept it when the positions are reversed. The rule needs no revelation and no shared religion, which is why it turns up independently in almost every literate culture, and it gives a stranger common moral ground in any era. Its radical step is the scope of 'others': extended beyond kin, city, faith and rank to every human being, it becomes an argument against slavery, persecution and cruelty. The player should quote the local version (Confucius, Hillel, the Gospel, a hadith) rather than import a foreign one.
- Pitfalls:
  - Claiming it for one religion or presenting it as a modern discovery; every audience already has its own wording
  - Ignoring that tastes differ: the refined version asks what the other person would want, in their situation
  - Assuming that people who recite it apply it to outsiders, slaves, heretics or enemies; historically most did not
  - Equating it with Kant's categorical imperative, which Kant explicitly distinguished from it
- History: egypt: c. 1850 BC – Tale of the Eloquent Peasant has a reciprocity maxim (reading disputed); Late Period papyrus (c. 4th c. BC): 'that which you hate to be done to you, do not do to another'; china: c. 500 BC – Confucius: 'what you do not wish for yourself, do not do to others' (Analects 15.24); c. 430 BC Mozi's impartial care for all; india: c. 400 BC–400 AD – Mahabharata: do not do to another what is disagreeable to yourself; Buddhist and Jain texts likewise; greece: c. 4th c. BC – versions in Isocrates and attributed to earlier sages; mesopotamia: c. 20 BC – Hillel, trained in Babylonia: 'what is hateful to you, do not do to your fellow' (recorded in the Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 31a); rome: 1st c. AD – Gospel form 'do to others as you would have them do to you' (Matthew 7:12); Seneca applies it to slaves; islamic: 7th c. – hadith: none of you believes until he wishes for his brother what he wishes for himself; europe: 1785 – Kant's universalisation test; the test asks whether a maxim could be a universal law; americas: 1993 – the Parliament of the World’s Religions in Chicago endorses the golden rule in its Declaration Toward a Global Ethic
- Read:
  - Confucius, Analects 15.24
  - Jeffrey Wattles, The Golden Rule (1996)
  - Harry J. Gensler, Ethics and the Golden Rule (2013)
